reason: The sources provide over 15 consistent claims including technical specifications, the history of its advocacy, and details on the optical artifacts.
story: On Valentine’s Day 1990, Voyager 1 looked back from approximately 4 billion miles away to capture a final 'Family Portrait' of our solar system. At the urging of astronomer Carl Sagan, the probe photographed Earth from 32 degrees above the ecliptic plane. The resulting image, the 'Pale Blue Dot,' shows our entire planet as a tiny speck occupying just 0.12 of a single pixel. While the dramatic beam of light Earth sits in looks like a celestial phenomenon, it is actually an optical artifact caused by sunlight reflecting off the camera’s internal hardware. NASA originally resisted the photo, fearing the Sun’s glare would destroy the spacecraft’s cameras and noting the shot had no scientific value. Once the 60-frame sequence was complete, mission control powered down the cameras forever to conserve energy for Voyager’s journey into interstellar space. It remains the most distant image of home ever taken.
angle: The iconic 'sunbeam' that Earth sits in is actually an optical artifact caused by sunlight reflecting off the camera's own internal parts.

claims.claim: Voyager 1 took the Pale Blue Dot photograph on February 14, 1990.
The photograph was taken from a distance of approximately 4 billion miles (6 billion kilometers).
Earth's size in the photograph is less than one pixel, specifically 0.12 of a pixel.
The light bands in the image are artifacts caused by sunlight reflecting off the camera and its sunshade.
The photograph was part of a larger 'Family Portrait' sequence consisting of 60 frames.
The image was captured from a vantage point approximately 32 degrees above the ecliptic plane.
Astronomer Carl Sagan was the primary advocate for the photograph, proposing it as early as 1981.
Carolyn Porco independently proposed taking a 'goodbye' image of Earth in the mid-1980s.
NASA initially rejected the photo because it lacked scientific value and risked camera damage.
Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object in existence.
NASA commanded Voyager 1 to power down its cameras permanently after the Family Portrait was taken.
The planetary sequence included Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.
Mars was not visible in the final sequence because it was obscured by scattered sunlight.
Mercury was missing from the portrait of the solar system.
Calculating the exposure for Earth was difficult because it was smaller than a pixel.
NASA released a remastered version of the image for its 30th anniversary in 2020.
Sagan famously described the Earth in the photo as a 'mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam.'

disputed: The exact distance to Earth is cited as 3.7 billion miles (6.055 billion km) in S1 but 4 billion miles (6.4 billion km) in S5 and S7. A script should use 'approximately 4 billion miles.'
The number of planets captured is disputed; S4 claims seven of eight planets were captured, while S7 claims six major planets were captured, explicitly stating Mercury, Mars, and Pluto missed out.
